No, you're partly right, and in retrospect it's not that revolutionary. But there are some differences:

  • First and foremost, notice I said "horizontal". I'm talking one over, one under.
  • Address bar, bookmarks, tabs are all shown twice, sneaking away at your precious screen-space*.
  • It's bulky and cumbersome. You can't resize both windows with one draw (I'm talking about moving the "boundary" between them, but also about resising the "whole thing"), you can't minimize both at the same time, you can't pull them both to a different monitor at the same time (yes, I do have two monitors...)
  • It looks, at best, ugly-ish. Integrating it into chrome/whatever would allow them to make it look nice. Even on the left/right approach: you could have the toolbars melt together. Wouldn't that look amazing?
  • RAM-savings, keep only one webpage in RAM instead of two copies of the same (I'm assuming theoretically you can render two scroll-states from the same webpage-data?)
  • If the page is interactive, it's not really the same with two windows. Data you've entered in one won't be visible in the other. On the other hand, I'm just guessing that if the page is too dynamic and responsive, there might be issues with making this work. But maybe it could be turned off then?

*This can be fixed with careful placement of windows and usage of utilities to make certain windows stay on top even when they lose focus, but that's a lot of work for the user and a really non-flexible solution which by the way introduces other major issues. Believe me, I've tried.
